name: Markdown Online
tagline: A browser-based markdown editor with live preview and export to HTML, PDF and Word.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Markdown rendering is the most solved problem in web development: there are a dozen mature parsers and all of them run client side. Live preview, local autosave and HTML export are a couple of hours of work with an off the shelf editor component and a sanitizer. PDF is the browser print dialog plus print CSS you will fuss over for an afternoon. Word is the only genuinely annoying part, and even that is a library call away if you accept that complex tables and footnotes will come out slightly wrong. Nothing here needs a server, an account or a network, which is exactly why a personal copy is fine.
coreLoopDIY: A local single page editor that renders markdown live, saves drafts to your browser, and exports the result as HTML, print-to-PDF or a .docx file.
requirements: no API keys, no backend, no accounts
whatYouLose: Word export fidelity: nested tables, footnotes and code blocks will need hand tuning
PDF output via browser print is adequate, not typeset; no page headers, widow control or font embedding unless you build it
The polish layer: keyboard shortcuts, toolbar, paste-from-Word cleanup, image handling, drag and drop
Extras like mermaid diagrams, math, syntax highlighting themes and table of contents generation, each one a separate decision
Someone else maintaining the thing when a dependency breaks
moatNotes: The moat is being the tab people reach for, not the code. Ranking for 'markdown to word' is worth more than any feature in the editor.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because they do not want a build, they want a URL. The typical buyer is pasting a README or an AI-generated draft and needs a .docx for a colleague in the next ninety seconds, and a hosted tool that promises the text never leaves the browser is a completely reasonable thing to pay a small amount for. A self-hosted clone wins only if you convert often enough to care, or if you want the export pipeline wired into your own writing setup.
notes: Converters live or die on search traffic, not on code quality.
prompt:
Build a local, offline markdown editor and converter as a single page web app. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at runtime.

Stack, use exactly this:
- Vite + TypeScript, no framework
- CodeMirror 6 for the editor pane, markdown language mode enabled
- marked for parsing, DOMPurify for sanitizing rendered HTML
- docx (the npm package) for Word export
- No CSS framework, write plain CSS

Layout: two panes side by side, editor left, rendered preview right, with a thin top bar. Scroll sync between panes based on line ratio is good enough, do not over engineer it. Collapse to tabbed single column under 800px wide.

Features in scope:
- Live preview, debounced at 120ms
- Autosave the current document to localStorage on every change, restore on load
- A document list in localStorage: new, rename, delete, switch. Keep it simple, no folders
- Export HTML: download a standalone .html file with the sanitized body and inlined minimal CSS
- Export PDF: open a print-only view and call window.print(), with @media print CSS that sets margins, avoids page breaks inside code blocks and headings, and hides the app chrome
- Export Word: walk the parsed markdown token tree and emit a .docx via the docx package. Support headings 1-6, paragraphs, bold, italic, inline code, links, ordered and unordered lists, blockquotes, code blocks as monospace shaded paragraphs, horizontal rules, and simple tables. Skip anything else rather than crashing
- Import: drag a .md file onto the window to load it
- Keyboard: Cmd/Ctrl+B bold, Cmd/Ctrl+I italic, Cmd/Ctrl+K link, Cmd/Ctrl+S triggers HTML export

Out of scope, do not build: mermaid, LaTeX math, image uploads, cloud sync, sharing links, themes beyond light and dark.

Deliver: working `npm run dev`, a README explaining the export caveats (Word fidelity is approximate, PDF depends on the browser print engine), and no .env because nothing here needs secrets.
